newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Slow Australia rural recovery underway - survey.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Slow Australia rural recovery underway - survey.

text.p: The Queensland Farmers' Federation (QFF) said its latest quarterly survey of Queensland's rural industry showed a gradual recovery with a slow and erratic return to normal conditions.
For the first time time December 1992, the index of farm production had moved into positive figures, Graham Dalton, QFF executive director, said in a statement.
This meant that more farms reported normal or above normal performance than those recording below normal performance during the September quarter.
In the latest quarter, 54 percent reported normal or above normal performance, up by five percent on the June quarter.
Better seasonal conditions for many commodities underpinned the recovery, Dalton said.
However, falling grain prices had taken the gloss off the season and it was clear the recovery would be long and hard, he said.

A return to more normal rainfall patterns across most of the state during the September quarter consolidated prospects for substantial sugar and winter grain harvests and set the scene for substantial plantings of cotton, summer grain and vegetable

The survey confirmed optimism among strongly-performing dairy, grain-cotton, sugarcane and pig industries where higher prices and increased volumes of supply were the main factors contributing to success, the survey said.

Substantial increases in production of grains and sugarcane had restored producers business confidence although the majority of producers were concerned at declining prices, it said. Intensive livestock producers (dairy, pigs, chickens) remained optimistic but beef and wool producers were pessimistic about future prospects, it said.
"It will take many years before producers are back on their feet," Dalton said.
Large parts of Queensland remained affected by drought and low prices for cattle and wool meant the recovery under way was going to be very protracted, he said.
Debt levels were at last expected to stabilise and should start to improve, Dalton said.
After six years of drought, the number of farms at risk remained high, but the overall position was set to improve over time, he said.
The number of farms facing serious difficulty servicing debt had now fallen to 12 percent from 16 percent at the same time last year, he said.

The survey predicts a significant growth in use of labour over the next six months. Use of most other farm inputs including fertiliser, fuel and lubricants was also expected to increase with the slow recovery, he said.
